title: Life at the Molecular Scale
description: Brownian motion, thermal energy, and why biology is wet

concepts.title: Brownian Motion
concepts.contentHtml:
Pollen grains in water jiggle randomly — Robert Brown noticed this in 1827. Einstein explained it in 1905: the grains are being kicked by water molecules in random thermal motion.

The mean-square displacement of a Brownian particle scales linearly with time: ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt, where D is the diffusion coefficient.

Inside a cell, everything diffuses — proteins, ions, signaling molecules. Diffusion is fast over micron scales (milliseconds), slow over millimeter scales (minutes). This sets the size limit of cells.

concepts.title: k_B T as the Reference Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
Thermal energy at body temperature is k_B T ≈ 4 × 10⁻²¹ J ≈ 0.025 eV ≈ 2.5 kJ/mol.

Any energy comparable to k_B T gets randomly tapped by thermal fluctuations. Hydrogen bonds (a few k_B T) make and break constantly. Strong covalent bonds (~100 k_B T) are stable.

Many biological processes are tuned to operate near the k_B T scale — they exploit thermal noise rather than fight it. Molecular motors, ion channels, and protein folding all live in this regime.

concepts.title: Low Reynolds Number World
concepts.contentHtml:
For a bacterium swimming in water, Reynolds number is around 10⁻⁵. Inertia is negligible; viscous drag dominates.

Stop the flagellum and the bacterium stops within a few percent of its body length. There's no coasting; every motion costs work.

This is why bacteria use rotary flagella — straight reciprocating motion produces no net displacement at low Re (the 'scallop theorem'). They've found ways to break time-reversal symmetry that work in their viscous world.

title: Molecular Motors
description: How cells move, divide, and stay alive

concepts.title: Walking on Microtubules
concepts.contentHtml:
Kinesin is a molecular motor that walks along microtubules, hauling cargo (vesicles, organelles, mRNA). It takes ~8 nm steps, one ATP molecule per step.

Each step is forward more often than backward — a motor is a Brownian ratchet that uses ATP hydrolysis to bias random thermal motion in a chosen direction.

The motor's free-energy budget per step is about 80 pN·nm (~20 k_B T) — about 80% of the energy released by hydrolyzing one ATP. Remarkable thermodynamic efficiency.

concepts.title: Muscle Contraction
concepts.contentHtml:
Muscle is myosin — another motor protein — pulling on actin filaments. Each myosin head goes through a cycle: bind ATP, hydrolyze, attach to actin, swing through a 'power stroke', release.

Billions of myosin heads in one muscle act asynchronously, summed forces giving smooth contraction. Cross-bridge models match the macroscopic force-velocity relation.

A. V. Hill's force-velocity curve, derived in 1938, encoded all of this before any of the molecular details were known.

concepts.title: Rotary Motors — ATP Synthase
concepts.contentHtml:
ATP synthase is the world's smallest rotary motor — a turbine driven by a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. As protons flow down their gradient, they spin a rotor that mechanically twists the catalytic domain to make ATP.

Boyer and Walker won the 1997 Nobel for working out the mechanism. Direct observation of the rotation came shortly after via fluorescent tags.

Roughly 10²¹ rotations per second occur in your body — about 100 ATP per second per molecule of synthase. Together they generate your daily 50+ kg of ATP turnover.

title: Membranes & Ion Channels
description: Electrical engineering at the cell wall

concepts.title: The Lipid Bilayer
concepts.contentHtml:
Cell membranes are bilayers of phospholipid molecules — hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous phases inside and out, hydrophobic tails facing each other in the middle.

The bilayer is fluid (lipids diffuse laterally) but tough (about 5 nm thick, dielectric constant ~2). It's an excellent electrical insulator: ions can't cross without help.

Embedded proteins — channels, pumps, receptors — provide that help selectively, turning the membrane into a programmable electrical circuit.

concepts.title: Ion Channels
concepts.contentHtml:
Ion channels are pore-forming proteins that let specific ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) cross a membrane.

Selectivity is amazing: a K⁺ channel can pass K⁺ a thousand times faster than the smaller Na⁺. The trick is a selectivity filter that mimics the K⁺-water shell. MacKinnon got the 2003 Nobel for the K⁺-channel structure.

Channels can be voltage-gated, ligand-gated, or mechanosensitive. They open and close on millisecond timescales — perfect for nervous system timing.

concepts.title: The Action Potential
concepts.contentHtml:
A neuron's resting potential (~−70 mV) is set by K⁺ leak channels. A stimulus opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels — Na⁺ rushes in, depolarizing the membrane. Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open shortly after — K⁺ rushes out, repolarizing.

The Hodgkin-Huxley equations (1952) describe this beautifully and match nerve recordings to fractions of a millivolt.

The action potential propagates along an axon as a regenerative wave at ~100 m/s in myelinated nerves. This is how you blink before getting hit in the eye.

title: Biomechanics
description: Forces and structures, from molecules to organisms

concepts.title: Allometric Scaling
concepts.contentHtml:
Why is an elephant proportioned differently from a mouse? Because forces and surfaces don't scale the same way as volumes.

If you double the linear size, the volume (and weight) goes up 8×, but cross-sectional bone area only 4×. So bones must thicken disproportionately.

Many biological quantities scale as power laws of body mass M: metabolic rate ~ M^(3/4), heart rate ~ M^(-1/4), lifespan ~ M^(1/4). These persist across many orders of magnitude.

concepts.title: DNA as a Polymer
concepts.contentHtml:
A DNA molecule is a long charged polymer with persistence length about 50 nm — much longer than its 2-nm diameter.

Stretching DNA with optical tweezers gives a force-extension curve perfectly fit by the worm-like chain model. At a critical tension (~65 pN), DNA undergoes a structural transition (overstretching).

Single-molecule experiments now routinely measure the forces that polymerases, helicases, and chromatin-remodeling enzymes exert — turning biophysics into a quantitative force-and-step science.

concepts.title: Cell Mechanics
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells aren't bags of liquid — they have a cytoskeleton (actin, microtubules, intermediate filaments) that gives them shape, strength, and active force-generating capability.

Mechanical signals from the cell's environment (substrate stiffness, applied stretch) influence gene expression, differentiation, and disease. Cancer cells often have abnormal mechanical properties.

The field of mechanobiology studies how mechanical inputs become biological outputs — a frontier where physics and medicine meet.

title: Quantum Biology & Frontier
description: Where quantum mechanics actually matters in living things

concepts.title: Photosynthesis & Quantum Coherence
concepts.contentHtml:
Photosynthesis transfers energy from absorbed photons to a reaction center with near 100% efficiency — through a forest of pigment molecules.

Experiments suggest quantum coherence may help: the energy explores multiple paths in superposition, finding the most efficient one before being measured by the environment.

How long this coherence lives in a warm, wet system has been controversial. But the fact that quantum effects might play a role in everyday biology is itself remarkable.

concepts.title: Bird Navigation & Radical Pairs
concepts.contentHtml:
European robins detect Earth's magnetic field for migration. The leading hypothesis: a radical-pair mechanism in cryptochrome proteins in the bird's eye.

Photoexcitation creates a pair of radicals whose spins are quantum-correlated. The Earth's weak magnetic field affects the singlet/triplet ratio enough to influence the chemical product, and somehow that signal gets to the brain.

This is one of very few clear cases where a macroscopic biological effect would directly require quantum spin physics.

concepts.title: Frontiers
concepts.contentHtml:
Active matter: collections of self-propelled units (cells, robots, swarms) that show emergent collective dynamics — flocks, schools, biofilms.

Soft active gels describe the cytoskeleton as a contractile, restructuring active material — explaining cell crawling and tissue mechanics.

Single-molecule everything: cryo-EM, super-resolution microscopy, and single-molecule fluorescence are turning biology into a quantitative science of individual molecular events. Biophysics is one of the most rapidly growing parts of physics.
